content: 1. Increased radon concentrations have been observed in thermally retrofitted buildings, raising concerns about potential health risks. This issue was explored in a study published in Radiation Protection Dosimetry (2014), which highlights the need for careful monitoring and mitigation strategies in energy-efficient housing. 2. The relationship between cold spells and health outcomes, including prevention and warning systems, was examined by Laaidi et al. in Public Health (2013). The study emphasizes the importance of public health interventions to reduce morbidity and mortality during extreme cold weather events. 3. Liddell and Guiney (2015) investigated the mental health impacts of living in cold and damp homes. Their findings, published in Public Health, provide a framework for understanding how inadequate housing conditions contribute to poor mental well-being. 4. Lloyd et al. (2008) explored the effects of improving the thermal quality of cold housing on blood pressure and general health. Their research, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, suggests that better insulation and heating can lead to significant health benefits. 5. Madden et al. (2014) conducted a mixed-methods evaluation of the Warm Homes, Healthy People fund, demonstrating the positive health outcomes associated with improved home heating. This study was published in Public Health. 6. Maidment et al. (2014) performed a meta-analysis on the health impacts of household energy efficiency measures. Their findings, published in Energy Policy, indicate that such interventions can lead to improved health outcomes, particularly in vulnerable populations. 7. Mercer (2003) highlighted the underestimated health risks associated with cold exposure in a study published in Environmental Research. The research underscores the need for greater awareness and preventive measures to address cold-related health issues. 8. Mesa-Frias et al. (2013) assessed the framing assumptions in quantitative health impact assessments, using housing interventions as an example. Their study, published in Environment International, provides insights into the methodological challenges of evaluating housing-related health outcomes. 9. Nahya (2002) reviewed the link between cold exposure and cardiovascular disease risk in the International Journal of Circumpolar Health. The review emphasizes the physiological mechanisms by which cold stress exacerbates cardiovascular conditions. 10. Norman et al. (1986) investigated the respiratory function of children living in homes insulated with urea-formaldehyde foam insulation. Their findings, published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, raise concerns about potential respiratory health risks associated with certain insulation materials. 11. Osman et al. (2010) conducted a randomized trial on the impact of home energy efficiency improvements in elderly patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Published in the European Respiratory Journal, the study demonstrates the health benefits of such interventions. 12. Platt et al. (2007) evaluated the Scottish Executive Central Heating Programme, assessing its health impacts. Their findings, published as research findings by the Scottish Executive, highlight the program's success in improving health outcomes through better heating systems. 13. Poortinga et al. (2017) analyzed the social and health outcomes of upgrades to national housing standards in a multilevel study published in BMC Public Health. The research demonstrates the broad benefits of housing improvements on population health. 14. Preval et al. (2017) examined the impact of improved insulation and heating on mortality risk among older adults with prior cardiovascular or respiratory hospitalizations. Their study, published in BMJ Open, underscores the life-saving potential of housing interventions. 15. Rivier et al. (2014) conducted a preliminary investigation into fungal contamination in homes in Lorraine, France. Published in the Revue Française d'Allergologie, the study highlights the health risks associated with indoor mold exposure. 16. Santamouris et al. (2014) studied indoor environmental quality in low-income households during winter in Athens. Their findings, published in Energy and Buildings, reveal the challenges faced by economically disadvantaged populations in maintaining healthy indoor environments. 17. Shortt and Rugkasa (2007) explored the link between fuel poverty and ill health in Northern Ireland. Their study, published in Health Place, provides evidence for the health benefits of housing interventions aimed at reducing fuel poverty. 18. Somerville et al. (2000) investigated whether installing heating systems in homes improves the health of children with asthma. Their findings, published in Public Health, suggest significant health improvements following such interventions. 19. Sowden and White (2014) conducted a qualitative study on the effects of social housing improvements on the health and well-being of residents in high-rise flats. Their findings were presented in The Lancet. 20. Spear et al. (2012) examined the presence of asbestos-contaminated vermiculite attic insulation and its potential for contaminating living spaces. Published in the Journal of Environmental Health, the study highlights the importance of addressing asbestos risks in residential settings. 21. Tavernier et al. (2006) conducted the IPEADAM study, which investigated indoor endotoxin exposure and its relationship with family status and housing characteristics. Published in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, the study provides insights into the health impacts of indoor environmental factors. 22. Telfar Barnard et al. (2011) evaluated the health service utilization and costs associated with retrofitted insulation and new heaters in New Zealand. Their findings, reported to the Ministry of Economic Development, demonstrate the economic and health benefits of such interventions. 23. Thomson et al. (2013) reviewed housing improvements for health and associated socio-economic outcomes in The Cochrane Library. The review highlights the evidence supporting the health benefits of housing interventions. 24. Valsecchi (2014) discussed the role of preventive measures in reducing health inequalities in Annali dell'Istituto Superiore di Sanità. The study emphasizes the importance of addressing housing-related health disparities. 25. Vandentorren et al. (2006) analyzed risk factors for death among elderly people living at home during the 2003 heatwave in France. Published in the European Journal of Public Health, the study underscores the vulnerability of older adults to extreme heat. 26. Viggers et al. (2013) described the aims and methods of a randomized community-based trial for people with COPD, focusing on warm homes for older adults. Published in BMC Public Health, the study highlights the potential health benefits of improved housing conditions. 27. Wilson et al. (2014) investigated whether residential energy conservation improves health in a study published in Energy Efficiency. The findings suggest that energy-efficient housing can lead to better health outcomes. 28. Windle et al. (2006) examined housing-related difficulties and their impact on health status among older people in Wales. Published in Health Place, the study highlights the importance of addressing housing issues to improve health outcomes. 29. Yarmoshenko et al. (2014) studied indoor radon problems in energy-efficient multi-story buildings. Published in Radiation Protection Dosimetry, the research emphasizes the need for radon mitigation in modern housing designs.
